pages.text: Gods of the World

image.note: Cover: four skies, four gods, one horizon

pages.text: Contents. Why We Made Gods / The Gods of Greece / The Gods of the North / The Gods of Nigeria / What All Myths Share.

Long before science, people looked up at the world and asked questions. Why does thunder crack? Why does the sun cross the sky? Why do people die? They did not have our answers. So they told stories, and in those stories, the answers wore the faces of gods.

image.note: Ancient people around a fire, storm above

pages.text: Almost every people on earth did this. They imagined powerful beings behind the wind, the harvest, the sea, and the storm. This book visits three great families of gods, from Greece, from the cold north, and from Nigeria, and then asks what they all have in common.
A myth is not just a made-up tale. A myth is a story a whole people once believed, told to explain the world and to teach how to live in it.

Imagine you had never been taught about clouds or electricity. A storm would be terrifying and strange. The sky roars. Light splits the air. Now imagine someone says: that is a god, up there, striking his mighty hammer. Suddenly the storm has a face, and a reason.

That is what gods did. They turned a frightening, puzzling world into a world of stories: powerful, but understandable. Every crop, every season, every sickness had a god behind it who could be pleased, or angered.

image.note: Farmer looking anxiously at the sky

pages.text: People built temples to these gods, sang to them, and left them gifts, hoping for rain, for a good harvest, for safety at sea. In return, the myths gave people something priceless: a way to feel less alone in a vast and mysterious world.

Picture a night long ago. No electric light, no science books. A family sits close as a storm shakes the roof, and a grandmother begins: "Let me tell you why the sky is angry." This is how myths lived: spoken in the dark, passed from old to young, as real to them as the rain.
We will meet gods who are jealous, gods who are kind, gods who trick and steal and fall in love. That is the strange delight of myths. The gods behave exactly like people, only much, much bigger.

We begin in ancient Greece, whose gods are perhaps the most famous of all. The Greeks believed their gods lived high on Mount Olympus, above the clouds, feasting and arguing and meddling in the lives of people below.

Their king was Zeus, lord of the sky and the storm. When Zeus was angry, he hurled thunderbolts. He ruled the other gods, though he could not always control them, and certainly could not control his own temper.

His brother Poseidon ruled the sea, striking the water with a three-pronged spear to raise storms and shake the earth. Sailors feared him and begged for his mercy. Their other brother, Hades, ruled the silent world of the dead, below the ground.

image.note: Poseidon in the waves with his trident

pages.text: Among the goddesses, wise Athena guarded the city and the arts of peace and war. Swift Hermes, with wings on his sandals, carried messages between gods and people, and slipped in and out of trouble. Beautiful Aphrodite ruled love itself.

image.note: Athena with owl; Hermes with winged sandals

pages.text: The Greeks told a story about how their greatest city got its name. Two gods, wise Athena and Poseidon of the sea, both wanted the city for their own, so the people set them a contest: whoever gave the finer gift would win.

image.note: Athena and Poseidon before the people

pages.text: Poseidon struck the ground with his spear and a spring burst out, but its water was salt, and no one could drink it. Then Athena knelt and planted a small tree: the first olive tree, giving food, oil, and wood for ever. The people chose Athena, and named their city Athens in her honour.

image.note: Olive tree sprouting; the naming of Athens

pages.text: The Greeks explained the seasons with a god-story too. Demeter, goddess of the harvest, had a daughter who was carried down to the world of the dead. In her grief, Demeter let the whole earth grow cold and bare.

image.note: Demeter mourning in a dead field

pages.text: A bargain was struck: the daughter would return for part of each year, and stay below for the rest. When she comes back, her mother rejoices and the world turns green. When she leaves, the cold returns. That, said the Greeks, is why we have summer and winter.

image.note: Split image: green spring, bare winter

pages.text: The Greek gods were powerful, but they were not perfect. They were proud, jealous, and quick to quarrel. And that was the point. Through them, the Greeks told stories about being human, its courage and its foolishness, on a giant stage in the sky.

image.note: Gods feasting and arguing on Olympus

pages.text: Now travel far to the cold north of Europe, to the lands of the Norse: the people we sometimes call the Vikings. Their world was ice, sea, and long dark winters, and their gods were as tough as the land that made them.

The Norse gods lived in a realm called Asgard, joined to the world of people by Bifrost, a flaming rainbow bridge across the sky. When you see a rainbow, said the Norse, you are looking at the road to the gods.

Their ruler was Odin, one-eyed and wise, who gave up his own eye in exchange for wisdom. He was god of knowledge, poetry, and war, and two ravens flew the world each day to whisper to him all they had seen.

But the most beloved was his son Thor, god of thunder. Thor was enormous and strong, with a red beard and a temper, and he carried a hammer that could level mountains and always flew back to his hand. The rumble of thunder was Thor's chariot rolling across the sky.

image.note: Thor swinging his hammer, storm behind

pages.text: The best Norse story of all begins with a disaster. Thor woke one morning to find his mighty hammer gone, stolen by a giant who would only give it back on one condition: that a goddess be sent to marry him.

The gods hatched a daring, ridiculous plan. They dressed Thor himself as the bride, in a veil and a gown, and sent him to the giant's hall with sly Loki beside him, disguised as a maid. Thor was furious. He went anyway.

image.note: Thor in a bridal veil, Loki grinning

pages.text: At the feast the giant grew suspicious, for his bride ate a whole ox and drank barrels dry, and her eyes blazed under the veil. But clever Loki whispered an excuse for every strange thing, until at last the hammer was carried in to bless the wedding, and laid in the bride's lap.

image.note: The hammer placed in Thor's lap

pages.text: That was the giant's mistake. Thor seized his hammer, threw off the veil, and the trick was over in a flash of thunder. The gods went home laughing. It is a story the Norse loved: even the mightiest god brought low, then saved by a joke and a quick wit.

And then there was Loki: not quite a god, not quite an enemy. Loki was the trickster, clever and sly, forever getting the gods into trouble and then, sometimes, out of it again. Half the best Norse stories begin with Loki grinning at a bad idea.

Loki was forever like this: the spark behind half the trouble and half the rescues in Asgard. He could change his shape into a fish, a fly, even a horse. The gods could not live with him, and could not manage without him. Every family, perhaps, knows someone a little like Loki.

The Norse were brave partly because of what they believed came next. Warriors who died bravely, they said, were carried to a great hall to feast until the last battle at the end of the world. Even their gods, they believed, would one day fall. A god who can die makes a people fearless.

image.note: Great feasting hall of fallen warriors

pages.text: Now come home, to Nigeria, whose peoples told god-stories as rich as any on earth, and still remember them today. Here too the thunder had a face, the harvest had a guardian, and the sky had a ruler.

Among the Yoruba, above all the gods stood Olorun, owner of the sky, so great and distant that people rarely prayed to him directly. Nearer to daily life were the orisha: powerful spirits, each with their own domain, their own colours, their own drumbeats.

image.note: Yoruba shrine, bright cloth and beads

pages.text: Fiercest of the orisha was Sango, god of thunder and lightning. Once a mighty king, he became the storm itself. When lightning strikes, the Yoruba remember Sango, and his double-headed axe flashing across the sky.

image.note: Sango with a double axe, lightning

pages.text: The Yoruba tell how Sango became the storm. He was once a mighty king, proud and powerful, with the strange gift of calling down fire from the sky. But his own power frightened even him, and in the end he left his throne and vanished.

His people looked up, and where he had gone they saw lightning split the clouds and heard his voice in the thunder. Their king had not died, they said. He had become the storm itself. And so, to this day, when thunder rolls over Yorubaland, the old people nod and say the storm-king has come home.

image.note: Lightning over the land, people looking up

pages.text: Where Sango was fire, Osun was water: the orisha of the river, of sweetness, love, and healing. People still gather at her river each year to honour her. Ogun, orisha of iron, watched over blacksmiths, hunters, and anyone who worked with metal.

The Igbo people, to the east, honoured Ala, goddess of the earth itself: the ground beneath your feet, the source of crops, and the keeper of right and wrong. To break a serious law was to offend Ala herself. Above all was Chukwu, the great creator.

The Igbo say the earth goddess Ala remembers everything: every child born, and every deed done, kind or cruel, is kept in the memory of the earth herself. To live well, they say, is to keep faith with Ala, on whose broad back we all walk.

And thunder in Igbo belief belonged to Amadioha, god of the sky and justice, whose anger flashed as lightning. Notice something remarkable. Greece had its thunder-god. The north had Thor. Nigeria has Sango and Amadioha. Across the whole world, the same great storm cried out for the same kind of god.

These are not dusty, forgotten tales. The orisha are still honoured, in Nigeria and far across the sea in Brazil, Cuba, and beyond, carried there long ago and never let go. Nigeria's gods are among the most alive in all the world.

Three families of gods. Greece on its bright mountain, the north on its rainbow bridge, Nigeria with its orisha and its earth. They grew up thousands of miles apart, and never met. Yet look how they rhyme.

Each has a ruler of the sky. Each has a god of the storm, hurling thunder: Zeus, Thor, Sango, Amadioha. Each explains the harvest and the seasons. Each has tricksters, and lovers, and quarrels. All around the world, people asked the same questions, and their answers came out strangely alike.

Why so similar? Because everywhere, people faced the same great mysteries: the storm, the harvest, love, and death. The same questions, asked under different skies, drew out the same kinds of stories. Myths are a mirror. In them, every people drew a picture of what it feared, admired, and longed to understand.

image.note: The same storm over four lands

pages.text: We tell these stories still, not because we believe the thunder is a hammer or an axe, but because the stories are magnificent, and because they are ours: the oldest, boldest guesses of the human family about the world it woke up in.

image.note: Child reading a book of myths

pages.text: So the next time thunder rolls, you will know a secret. Somewhere, long ago, someone heard that same sound and reached for a story. A Greek heard Zeus. A Norseman heard Thor. A Yoruba child heard Sango. And now you hear all three at once.

image.note: Child at a window, storm outside, smiling

pages.text: Gods to know. Zeus, Greek king of the sky. Poseidon, Greek sea. Odin, Norse wisdom. Thor, Norse thunder. Loki, Norse trickster. Olorun, Yoruba sky. Sango, Yoruba thunder. Osun, Yoruba river. Ala, Igbo earth. Amadioha, Igbo thunder.
Three peoples here, but every land on earth has its gods: Egypt, India, China, the Americas, and more. Each sky, its own stories. Which will you listen for next?
